items.title: Edward Jenner did not invent inoculation
items.claim: What did Edward Jenner demonstrate in 1796?

options.text: The first prevention of smallpox in human history
That deliberate infection with cowpox (vaccinia) protected against smallpox — a safer alternative to existing variolation (deliberate infection with smallpox itself)
That smallpox could be cured after infection

items.reveal:
Variolation — inoculation with smallpox itself — was practised in China, India, the Ottoman Empire and West Africa centuries before Jenner. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought it to Britain from Constantinople in 1721. It worked but killed around 1-2% of those treated.

Jenner's experiment on 14 May 1796 used pus from milkmaid Sarah Nelmes's cowpox sores, inoculated into 8-year-old James Phipps. Phipps was later challenged with smallpox and did not become ill.

Jenner published in 1798. The Vaccination Act 1853 made it compulsory in England. WHO declared smallpox eradicated on 8 May 1980.
items.why: The 'lone genius' narrative misses preceding practice. Jenner improved a known technique with a safer biological substitute — major progress, but not the first prevention.

items.title: Cholera transmission was solved by removing a pump handle
items.claim: In the 1854 Soho outbreak, what did John Snow do?

options.text: He developed the first cholera vaccine
He mapped deaths around Broad Street, identified the public water pump as the source, and persuaded authorities to remove its handle on 8 September 1854

items.reveal:
Snow's spot map of Broad Street showed deaths clustered around one pump. He overruled the dominant 'miasma' (bad air) theory of disease.

The pump handle was removed and cases fell. The cause was a leaking cesspit contaminating the well. Snow published 'On the Mode of Communication of Cholera' in 1855 — but his germ theory was not widely accepted until the 1860s with Pasteur and Koch.

London's main response was Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system (1859-1875), built largely after the 'Great Stink' of 1858 made Parliament unbearable.
items.why: Public health is often credited to grand theories. The 1854 case shows that careful observation and a map could outperform the dominant medical theory of the day — even before the underlying biology was understood.

items.title: Britain ran on local solar time until the railways forced standardisation
items.claim: When did Britain adopt a single national time?

options.text: Railway companies adopted Greenwich Mean Time from 1840 (Great Western) to coordinate timetables; legal national time followed by the Definition of Time Act 1880
Not until the 1950s when broadcasting required it

items.reveal:
Before railways, towns kept local solar time — Bristol was about 10 minutes behind London by the sun. Railway timetables made this unworkable. The Great Western Railway adopted GMT in 1840; most railways followed by 1848.

Local authorities resisted; the Exchange Clock at Bristol famously had two minute hands. The Definition of Time Act 1880 standardised legal time. The International Meridian Conference (Washington, 1884) set Greenwich as the prime meridian for the world.
items.why: The 'natural' experience of time is local. Industrial systems forced its standardisation — the railway is one of the first technologies to remake the perception of time itself.
